questions.title: If the defendant instigated the creation of the videos, how can his later use still be "transformative" fair use?
questions.question_body: The opinion rejects Santos’s argument that Kimmel can’t claim transformation because he "instigated the creation" of the Cameo videos by submitting the prompts. The panel instead applies a reasonable observer standard (citing Warhol) and says the JKL segments had a different purpose—commenting on Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money—than the videos’ original purpose of encouragement/positivity. I’m confused how the instigator point fits: If Kimmel designed the prompts to elicit specific statements, doesn’t that make the original purpose the same as his later use? Does it matter that Santos contends his original purpose aligned with Kimmel’s (i.e., to say what the buyer asked for, for money)? How do courts cabin manipulation of the "original" purpose by the secondary user when assessing transformation?

questions.title: Does deception in obtaining a work (fake names, misrepresentations) negate fair use after Harper & Row?
questions.question_body: Santos argued that Kimmel’s fake-name Cameo requests show bad faith that should nullify fair use. The panel says Harper & Row’s "fair use presupposes good faith" language has been distanced from, and emphasizes defendants’ purpose as commentary/criticism rather than market substitution. What is the current Second Circuit (and Supreme Court) view on whether bad faith or deception can weigh against, or defeat, fair use? Is there a meaningful distinction between deception used to scoop or supplant a market (e.g., unpublished manuscript in Harper & Row) and deception used to facilitate commentary? How do courts weigh bad faith under factor one versus treating it as irrelevant?

questions.title: How can fair use be decided on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion—what materials can the court consider at the pleadings stage?
questions.question_body: The court affirms dismissal because fair use was clear from the complaint and the works themselves, citing TCA Television and Cariou. Procedurally, what has to be in or attached to the complaint (or incorporated by reference) to let a court consider the original Cameo videos and the JKL segments on a 12(b)(6) motion? Can the court take judicial notice of the videos if they are publicly available online, or must they be exhibits? The panel also took notice of copyright registrations—are there limits on using registration data (e.g., publication dates) at this stage to resolve factor-two issues?

questions.title: Why doesn’t broadcasting Cameo videos on TV create cognizable market harm under factor four?
questions.question_body: On market effect, the panel quotes Hachette and Campbell and says the relevant question is usurpation of a substitutive market, not harm from criticism. But Santos sells personalized videos; couldn’t there be a licensing market for re-broadcasting those videos or for creating similar sponsored content? How do courts distinguish between (a) a genuine, substitutive licensing market for using the plaintiff’s videos on TV and (b) a non-cognizable market for licensing criticism or lampooning? Does it matter that Cameo or Santos might offer licenses for media use in non-critical contexts?

questions.title: How did the "nature of the work" factor apply where the videos are creative but were "published the same day"?
questions.question_body: The panel notes that the copyright registrations show the videos were published the same day they were created and cites 17 U.S.C. § 101. I’m trying to understand the factor-two analysis: Are these Cameo videos considered highly creative (which would weigh against fair use) but with the "published" status mitigating that? How exactly does "publication" under § 101 get determined from the registration record, and why does being published matter here if the works are otherwise expressive and personalized?

questions.title: Why couldn’t Santos enforce Cameo’s user Terms of Service as a third-party beneficiary under Illinois law?
questions.question_body: For the direct breach claim, the court applies Illinois law and says there’s a strong presumption against third-party beneficiaries unless the contract "practically" says so expressly. Santos argued Kimmel (a user) breached the TOS that users agree to, but the panel says there’s nothing close to an express declaration granting Santos enforcement rights, and notes other provisions do have explicit third-party language. Practically speaking, what sort of language would have been sufficient to let a Cameo creator like Santos enforce user TOS? Does the presence of some express third-party clauses elsewhere in the TOS create a negative inference against implied third-party status for creators?

questions.title: Why did New York law govern the implied-in-fact contract claim, and what "essential terms" had to be pleaded?
questions.question_body: The court analyzes the implied-in-fact contract claim under New York law (citing Rocky Point, Caniglia, DG & A), while applying Illinois law to the express TOS claim. What choice-of-law principles explain that split—was it because the TOS had an Illinois choice-of-law clause but the alleged implied agreement arose in New York? Substantively, what specific "essential terms" would Santos have needed to allege non-conclusorily to state an implied contract with Kimmel (e.g., no broadcast use, no commercial exploitation, price adjustments), and how would a "meeting of the minds" be shown if there was no explicit discussion beyond the standard Cameo transaction?

questions.title: What qualifies as "out-of-pocket" loss for fraudulent inducement in New York when the plaintiff was paid for the work?
questions.question_body: For the fraud claim, the panel (citing Lama Holding and Connaughton) says Santos failed to allege any out-of-pocket loss. If Santos was paid Cameo’s fee but alleges he was tricked into making videos for a purpose he wouldn’t have agreed to (national broadcast mockery), what types of damages could count as out-of-pocket in New York? Could time and effort, foregone opportunities, or costs to remediate reputational harm ever qualify? If benefit-of-the-bargain is unavailable in fraud, are rescission, restitution, or unjust enrichment viable alternatives on similar facts, or do those fail for the same reasons?
